 Walmart Zelda Switch 2: $519.99 Gift Card, 48 Hours [2026]
 Ryan Cole 
 Updated Nov 3, 2026 · 16 min read 
 Walmart reportedly canceled some pre-orders for the Nintendo Switch 2 “The Legend of Zelda” 40th Anniversary Edition and is now supposedly sending $519.99 eGift cards to affected buyers, according to Nintendo Life . As of November 3, 2026, the story rests on customer emails and press reports rather than a public Walmart statement.

 The details matter here, because the offer has two parts. One is a gift card equal to the console’s reported price. The other is an “Exclusive Reservation” that lets some customers reorder the console, and Kotaku frames that second offer around a 48-hour window.
 This analysis sorts what the reports say from what nobody has confirmed. It also looks at why a retailer would cancel a hot pre-order, how the compensation compares with other ways of fixing the mistake, and what the episode says about a Switch 2 market that has already lost some of its early sales momentum .

 Add now Walmart Zelda Switch 2 Cancellations: The Short Version
 Reports describe a simple chain of events. Customers pre-ordered the Zelda 40th Anniversary Edition of the Switch 2 through Walmart at a reported price of $519.99. Some of those orders then got canceled. The cancellation emails reportedly called the move “in error.”
 A follow-up email from Walmart, as relayed by customers, reportedly said affected buyers would receive a Walmart eGift Card for $519.99. The same reporting says the card should land by email within 10 business days. Nintendo Life carries that timeline, and Gaming Route covers the same offer under a headline that pairs the gift card with a 48-hour reorder.

 Some customers also reportedly got an Exclusive Reservation, which opens a 48-hour window to reorder the same console. Not everyone appears to get both offers. No outlet has established the exact rules, and Walmart has not published an official breakdown of who qualifies for what.
 The headline number is clean: $519.99 in, $519.99 back. Everything around that number is murkier, and the rest of this piece takes it apart.
 What the Cancellation Emails Reportedly Say
 The first email customers describe is the cancellation notice. Per the reports, Walmart told buyers their Zelda-edition Switch 2 pre-orders were canceled and described the cancellation as “in error.” That phrase is the only wording in this story that outlets quote directly from Walmart’s messages, and it is brief.
 “In error” can mean several things. It could point to an inventory counting mistake, a system fault that accepted more orders than stock allowed, or a pricing or listing glitch. The reports do not say which, and Walmart has not clarified. Treat any more specific explanation as speculation.
 What the wording does tell us is how Walmart chose to frame the problem. Calling a cancellation an error signals that the company views the customer as the wronged party. That framing usually precedes some form of make-good, and a make-good is what customers say arrived next.
 Stevivor headlined its own report around the same sequence: cancellations described as an error, followed by an offer of a reservation and a gift card. Multiple outlets arriving at the same sequence from customer emails strengthens the picture, though it does not replace an official statement.
 The $519.99 eGift Card: What Is Reported
 The gift card is the part that drew the headlines. Reports say affected customers were told they would receive a Walmart eGift Card for $519.99, matching the console’s reported price. Notebookcheck uses the word “promised” in its headline, which is the right level of caution.
 The delivery window is the next detail. The reported email says the card will arrive by email within 10 business days. Ten business days works out to two calendar weeks, so the latest a card should land for a buyer who got the email today is mid-November.
 Two things are not established. First, it is unclear whether every canceled customer qualifies. Second, no source has confirmed delivery to all eligible customers. The reports describe the cards as promised or reported by customers, and that distinction is the difference between an announcement and a completed payout.
 An eGift card is also not a refund. The original payment presumably returns through the normal cancellation process, so the gift card appears to be an extra on top of the money back. That reading fits the reports, though the fact that customers describe the card as matching the console price leaves room for confusion about whether it replaces or adds to the refund. Check your own email for the exact wording.
 The 48-Hour Exclusive Reservation
 The second offer looks more valuable to anyone who still wants the console. Some affected customers reportedly received an “Exclusive Reservation” that lets them reorder the Zelda 40th Anniversary Edition. The reported window is 48 hours.
 How the reorder window reportedly works
 Kotaku and others describe a two-day window for each customer, and the start time presumably follows the email. Buyers then have 48 hours to complete a purchase. Miss it, and the reservation lapses. The reports do not say what happens to the held unit afterward, but the logical outcome is that it returns to general inventory.
 A 48-hour limit protects Walmart from tying up scarce stock indefinitely. It also pressures customers to act fast, which is useful if the retailer wants to know quickly how many units it can release to everyone else.
 Who might get both offers
 The reports suggest the pairing varies by customer. Some people see both the reservation and the card. Others reportedly see only one. Because Walmart has not described its criteria, the cause is open. Order timing, account history, or the specific cancellation batch are all plausible, and none is confirmed.
 That uncertainty is why the next section exists. Readers deserve a plain split between what the sources support and what remains a guess.
 Confirmed vs Unconfirmed: A Claim-by-Claim Check
 The table below grades each claim by the evidence available today. “Reported” means named outlets relay it from customer emails. “Unconfirmed” means no source establishes it.
 Claim Status Basis 
 Walmart canceled some Zelda 40th Anniversary Switch 2 pre-orders Reported Customer emails relayed by Nintendo Life, Stevivor, Kotaku 
 Emails described the cancellations as “in error” Reported Customer emails relayed by press 
 Console price was $519.99 Reported Coverage of the pre-order listing 
 Affected customers get a $519.99 Walmart eGift Card Reported Customer email relayed by press 
 Gift card arrives within 10 business days Reported Customer email relayed by press 
 Some customers get an “Exclusive Reservation” to reorder Reported Customer emails relayed by press 
 Reorder window lasts 48 hours Reported Customer emails relayed by press 
 Every canceled customer qualifies for the card, the reservation, or both Unconfirmed No source establishes eligibility rules 
 Gift cards delivered to all eligible customers Unconfirmed Cards described as promised, not verified as delivered 
 Exact number of canceled pre-orders Unconfirmed No public figure 
 Walmart “oversold” the consoles Unconfirmed Reported, but no official Walmart statement 
 Seven rows carry the “reported” label and four carry “unconfirmed.” The reported rows all trace back to customer emails, which means a single underlying source type. That is common for consumer stories of this kind, and it is also why caution is warranted until Walmart speaks.
 Did Walmart Oversell the Zelda Switch 2?
 The oversold theory is the most common explanation floating around the coverage. The logic is straightforward: a retailer accepts more pre-orders than it has units, then cancels the surplus. Reports raise this idea, but there is no official Walmart statement confirming it.
 The evidence for the theory is circumstantial. Walmart canceled only some orders, not all. It called the cancellations an error. It then offered a reorder path to some customers, which suggests it either found additional stock or reshuffled allocation. None of that proves overselling, but it fits.
 Alternative explanations exist. A third-party seller on a marketplace listing could have failed to fulfill. A promotion could have fired against the wrong inventory pool. A supplier shipment could have come in short. Without Walmart’s account, the honest answer is that nobody outside the company knows.
 For readers, the practical takeaway does not depend on the cause. Whether the root problem was overselling, a glitch, or a supply gap, the remedy on offer is the same, and it is described in the same terms across outlets.
 Gift Card or Reorder: Which Offer Fits Which Buyer
 Because eligibility is unclear, the table below treats each combination as a possible scenario rather than a confirmed customer type. The “practical move” column is analysis, not Walmart guidance.
 Possible scenario Offer in the email Clock Practical move 
 Reservation and card Reorder access plus $519.99 eGift Card 48 hours to reorder, card within 10 business days Reorder first if you still want the console, then track the card 
 Reservation only Reorder access 48 hours Decide quickly, ask support whether a card applies 
 Card only $519.99 eGift Card Within 10 business days Hold the email, watch for the card, look at other retailers for the console 
 Neither Cancellation notice only None stated Contact Walmart support and keep screenshots 
 Reserved but passed on reorder Card may still arrive Card within 10 business days Confirm with support that skipping the reorder does not void the card 
 The last row is the one most likely to cause grief. Reports do not say whether declining or missing the reservation affects the gift card. Customers who plan to skip the reorder should ask before assuming the card is safe.
 How a Retailer Ends Up Canceling a Hot Pre-Order
 Large retailers run pre-orders on systems that track available quantity, reserved quantity, and promised ship dates. When a limited-edition console goes live, demand arrives in a spike. Systems that work fine on a normal Tuesday can misbehave under a flood of simultaneous checkouts.

 Zelda: Ocarina of Time Preorders Drop $10 to $59.99 [2026] 
 Limited editions add a second wrinkle. Allocation from the manufacturer is often fixed well before launch. If a retailer’s internal forecast and the real shipment disagree, the gap appears the moment units are due to ship. Reports place the cancellations in the run-up to delivery, which fits that pattern without proving it.
 This is a general description of how such failures occur, not a diagnosis of Walmart’s. The company has not explained its own system or allocation. Still, the pattern helps readers see why “in error” can be literally true even when the buyer’s frustration is entirely justified.
 A cancellation at the last minute also hits harder than one at the start. A buyer who ordered weeks ago may have planned a gift, turned down other retailers, or skipped a restock alert. The gift card reads as an attempt to price that lost time.
 Why the Gift Card Matches the Console Price
 Matching the card to the sticker price makes strategic sense. A $519.99 card puts the customer back in a position to buy the same product, or something comparable, without paying any more than they would have paid before. It turns the cancellation from a loss into a roughly neutral event.
 It also keeps the money inside Walmart. A gift card is store credit, so the customer who wants a different Switch 2 bundle , a game, or an unrelated purchase will likely spend it at the same retailer. For Walmart, the card costs less in real terms than its face value, since part of it may never be redeemed.
 That is a cynical read, and it is only one. Another is that Walmart wanted to make a visible goodwill gesture at the moment fans were most irritated. The reported 10-business-day delivery window suggests a process that runs in batches rather than instantly, which is consistent with a cleanup effort after the fact.
 Either way, the size of the gesture signals that Walmart treats the problem as its own. Compensation equal to the full price is a generous benchmark that other retailers will notice.
 Market Context: A Switch 2 Market Past Its Launch Rush
 The cancellation lands at an odd moment for Nintendo’s hardware. Earlier on this site, we covered how Switch 2 sales slipped 12% and lost the title of fastest-selling U.S. console in Circana’s data. Demand for the base console has cooled from launch-window levels even as collector editions stay scarce.
 That split explains the whole saga. A mainstream Switch 2 is easier to find, and discounting has started. Our report on the Switch 2 at $436 on AliExpress during early Black Friday shows how far third-party prices can drift below shelf price. A limited Zelda edition, by contrast, draws a different buyer who wants the design more than the discount.
 Software is feeding the demand, too. The Ocarina of Time remake has drawn heavy attention, and our coverage of the Ocarina of Time topping the Switch 2 eShop charts on November 1 shows how fast Zelda interest is building ahead of the game’s launch. A Zelda-themed console is the obvious hardware companion for that buyer.
 It is worth separating two kinds of Switch 2 customers. One group buys the cheapest available unit and plays whatever is on sale. The other wants the edition that matches a specific franchise moment. Retailers lose the second group’s trust when a pre-order vanishes, because that group planned around one specific box.
 For the wider category, our gaming section tracks the same pressure points: scarce collector editions on one side, falling prices for standard units on the other.
 How Walmart’s Fix Compares With Other Retailer Approaches
 Retailers have a short menu of options when they cancel a pre-order. The table below sets the four main approaches side by side. It is an analytical framework, so the cost and goodwill ratings are judgment calls, not measured data. Walmart’s reported approach combines the last two rows.
 Approach What the customer gets Retailer cost Goodwill effect 
 Refund only Original payment returned Lowest Weak, buyer is left with nothing 
 Refund plus small coupon Money back and a modest discount Low Mild, often seen as token 
 Refund plus priority reorder Money back and a short window to buy again Moderate, needs held stock Strong for buyers who still want the item 
 Refund plus full-price gift card Money back and store credit equal to the price Highest in headline terms Strong, signals the retailer owns the error 
 Walmart’s reported package stacks the reorder path on top of the full-price card for at least some buyers. That is the generous end of the menu. Whether it is sustainable depends on how many customers were affected, and the count has not been made public.

 Competitors face a quiet comparison. If another retailer cancels a hot pre-order in the next few weeks and offers only a refund, shoppers will point to Walmart’s gift card as the new standard. That raises the cost of any future stumble across the industry.
 History: Console Pre-Order Failures Are Not New
 Console launches have a long record of retailer trouble. Over successive hardware generations, buyers have reported canceled orders, listings that disappeared at checkout, delayed shipments, and duplicate charges. The causes range from bot traffic to allocation shortfalls to plain software bugs.
 What has changed is the speed of the response and the size of the make-good. Social media and gaming sites now carry screenshots of customer emails within hours, which pushes retailers to offer something concrete fast. A refund alone, once accepted as standard, now reads as the minimum.
 Nintendo-specific collector editions raise the stakes further. Fans treat anniversary hardware as an object of value, and secondary-market prices can climb well above retail. A buyer who loses a pre-order at $519.99 may face a much higher price to get the same unit from a reseller, which is part of why a card matching the original price feels fair but not fully compensatory.
 The pattern also connects to memory and component costs. We have written about Apple’s Ternus warning on unprecedented RAM costs , and the same supply tension affects how many consoles ship and where. Tight supply is the backdrop to many pre-order frustrations in 2026, though no source ties it to the Walmart cancellations specifically.
 What Affected Customers Should Do Now
 If Walmart canceled your Zelda Switch 2 pre-order, the steps below follow from the reports. They are practical suggestions, not instructions from Walmart.
 A short checklist
 Open the cancellation email and note the exact time the message was sent, because a 48-hour clock reportedly runs from it.
 Look for a second email mentioning an “Exclusive Reservation” and follow the steps in that message.
 If you still want the console, complete the reorder before the window closes.
 Screenshot every email and the cart page, since eligibility rules are unpublished.
 Track the $519.99 eGift Card for 10 business days and contact Walmart support if it does not show up.
 Confirm the original payment was refunded separately from the gift card.
 Do not assume the gift card is guaranteed because other buyers report receiving one. Reports describe cards as promised, and delivery to all eligible customers is not established. Keep your records until the card is in your account.
 If you decide against the reorder, use the card on something you will actually play. November is crowded with releases, and our rundown of 11 Switch games landing in November is a reasonable place to start spending.
 Four Predictions for the Walmart Zelda Saga
 These are analyst-style judgments, not reported facts. Each could be wrong, and we flag the assumptions behind them.
 Walmart will likely issue some public explanation. Press interest is high and the “oversold” claim remains unanswered. A short statement is the cheapest way to close the story.
 More customers will report that cards arrived, but a few will report problems. Any batch process this large produces stragglers. Expect complaints about late or missing cards around the 10-business-day mark.
 Other retailers will tighten limited-edition pre-order caps. Per-customer limits and queued checkouts are cheap to add, and a high-profile cancellation gives them a clear reason to do so.
 The Zelda edition will stay scarce through the Ocarina of Time launch window. Demand is tied to the game, and our Ocarina of Time remake review suggests the software will keep Zelda in the conversation.
 The common thread is accountability. When one large retailer sets a high bar for fixing a mistake, the others feel pressure to match it, and customers learn to expect it.
 What We Still Don’t Know
 Several basics remain unanswered. Nobody has published how many pre-orders Walmart canceled or how many customers qualify for compensation. No official statement addresses the oversold claim. No source verifies that cards reached every eligible customer.
 We also do not know whether the reorder reservations drew from newly found stock or from the same pool that caused the shortfall. If the former, Walmart may have solved the supply gap. If the latter, a second round of problems is possible.
 The takeaway: the story is real enough to act on and thin enough to hold loosely. Buyers should use the offers they have been given, document everything, and wait for Walmart to fill in the gaps.
 FAQ: Walmart Zelda Switch 2 Cancellations
 Did Walmart really cancel Zelda Switch 2 pre-orders?
 Reports from Nintendo Life, Stevivor, and Kotaku say Walmart canceled some pre-orders for the Nintendo Switch 2 “The Legend of Zelda” 40th Anniversary Edition. The exact number of canceled orders has not been made public.
 How much is the Walmart gift card worth?
 Reports say the Walmart eGift Card is worth $519.99, matching the console’s reported price. A customer email said it would arrive by email within 10 business days.
 What is the Exclusive Reservation?
 It is a reported offer that lets some affected customers reorder the console. The window reportedly lasts 48 hours, and buyers should read their own email for the exact steps.
 Do all canceled customers get the gift card?
 That is not established. Reports do not confirm that every canceled customer qualifies for the card, the reservation, or both, and Walmart has not published eligibility rules.
 Did Walmart oversell the console?
 Some coverage uses the word, but no official Walmart statement confirms it. The cancellation emails reportedly said only that the cancellations were “in error.”
 Is the gift card on top of my refund?
 Reports do not spell this out. The sensible reading is that the cancellation refund and the gift card are separate, but confirm it with Walmart support and check your payment method for the returned charge.
 What should I do if the gift card never arrives?
 Wait until the reported 10-business-day window has passed, then contact Walmart support with screenshots of the cancellation email, the compensation email, and your order number.
 Can I still buy the Zelda Switch 2 elsewhere?
 Availability varies by retailer and changes quickly. Reports describe the edition as scarce, so check official retailer listings rather than third-party resellers that charge a premium.
